h1: Learning about beer online: where a beginner should start
title: Learning about beer online | Craft Beer School
desc: A practical path for beginners: tasting, styles, ingredients and process, how to judge online courses and what a good first course covers.
teaser: The internet has endless beer content and very little order. Here is a sequence that works.
standfirst: You can learn a lot about beer without leaving home. The trick is order: taste first, then styles, then ingredients, then process. This guide sets out a path.
sections:
Beer content online ranges from brilliant to wrong. Beginners often jump into recipes, forum arguments and hop names without knowing what a good beer tastes like. That is like studying music theory without listening to music.

Start from the glass and work back to the brewery. You will understand explanations better when you know what they are explaining.

Another problem is that online beer advice is often written for one country or one climate. A tip about water or storage may be wrong where you live. Prefer sources that explain the reason behind a rule, so you can adjust it for your own situation.

Pick three or four different beers: a pale lager, a wheat beer, a pale ale and a stout. Pour each into a clean glass at the right temperature, smell, taste slowly and write a line. What did you notice first? Was it sweet, bitter, sour, roasty? Our how to taste beer guide gives a simple routine.

Drink in moderation, with water and food. Non-alcoholic beer works well for practising. Plenty of learners use it all the way through.

Write down what you taste. After a month you will have a personal vocabulary. You will see patterns in what you like. Beginners often find that they enjoy beers they thought they disliked once they know what to look for. Bitterness, for instance, is easier to enjoy when you recognise it as a balance to malt sweetness.

Styles are families of beer sharing ingredients and methods. You do not need to know them all. Learn the main branches: lager, ale, wheat, stout and sour. Then drill into one or two. Our beginner's map of world beer styles and the beer styles guide are good places to begin.

Do not try to memorise style guidelines. Learn what makes styles different: the grain bill, the yeast and the fermentation temperature. Lagers ferment cold, at about 8 to 13 °C (46 to 55 °F). They taste clean. Ales ferment warmer and often show fruit and spice from the yeast. That one difference explains a lot.

Beer has four main ingredients: water, malted barley, hops and yeast. Malt gives sugar, colour and body. Hops give bitterness and aroma. Yeast turns sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide and shapes flavour. Water carries everything and influences taste through its minerals.

The process runs from milling and mashing to boiling, fermenting, conditioning and packaging. Understanding each step explains most of what you taste in the glass, including faults. See beer off flavours for an example.
How to judge an online course

Ask a few questions before you pay:

  • Who teaches and have they worked in a brewery?
  • Is it live, so you can ask questions, or recorded only?
  • Is there practice, such as tasting assignments?
  • Are class sizes small?
  • What do you walk away with?

Avoid anything that promises to make you an expert in days. Skills in tasting and brewing come from repetition.
What a live online course gives you

A live course gives you a teacher who answers questions as they arise and other learners to compare notes with. It also gives you a schedule that keeps you going. Our courses run on Saturdays and Sundays, 12:00 PM to 2:00 PM India Standard Time (UTC+5:30). Students join from their own time zone and recordings cover a missed class. Classes are capped at 20 so questions get answered.

Questions in class are the biggest gain. A text or video cannot tell you why your own glass tastes odd. A teacher who has worked in breweries can.

Over a month you can taste a dozen beers with notes, understand the main style families and know how beer is made. That is a strong base. Pair your learning with food too: see pairing beer with Southeast Asian food for one example of how flavour works at the table.

Keep a simple log of what you tried each week. Review it after a month and pick the next step: a deeper look at one style, a first attempt at pairing or a live course if you want structure.
faqs: Can I learn about beer online?
Yes. Tasting, styles, ingredients and process can all be learned online, especially in a live course with tasting assignments.
What should a beginner learn first?
Start with tasting, then styles, then ingredients and process. Each step makes the next easier.
Do I need to drink alcohol to learn?
No. Non-alcoholic beers let you practise tasting. Many learners use them. Follow local law and drink responsibly.
How long does it take to get started?
A few weeks of regular tasting and study give you a solid base. Expertise takes much longer.
